analysis.one_liner: Cuts the estate tax to 20% on estates over $1 million and 30% above $10 million.
analysis.headline: The bill cutting estate tax rates on million-dollar estates was introduced in April 1997, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the estate tax rate schedule. Estates worth over $1 million would pay a flat 20% rate instead of the existing graduated rates that go up to 55%, and the portion of an estate above $10 million would be taxed at 30%. It would also raise the credit that shields the first slice of an estate and lift the estate-tax filing threshold from $600,000 to $1 million, meaning no estate under $1 million would owe the tax at all [S3]. It never got a hearing or a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to estates worth more than $1 million. Under the bill, a $3 million taxable estate would owe roughly $600,000 instead of a much larger graduated tax, and estates between $600,000 and $1 million would owe nothing. The largest estates — those over $10 million — would see their top marginal rate fall from 55% to 30% [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the graduated estate tax rates (which reached 55% on large estates) with a flat 20% rate on taxable amounts up to $10 million and a 30% rate on amounts above that [S2][S3].
Raises the unified credit against estate and gift taxes from $192,800 to $200,000, shielding a larger initial portion of every estate from tax [S3].
Raises the estate-tax filing threshold from $600,000 to $1,000,000, so estates under $1 million would no longer have to file or pay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury — meaning taxpayers generally. The estate tax is paid by roughly the largest 1-2% of estates, and cutting its rates means the lost revenue is made up by other taxpayers, by borrowing, or by smaller spending elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The benefits go almost entirely to the heirs of estates worth over $1 million, a small share of decedents; the largest estates, over $10 million, get the steepest rate cut — from 55% to 30% [S3].
The bill contains no revenue offset, so the cut would add to deficits or require higher taxes or lower spending on everyone else.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the main case against current law — that the tax falls on savings that were already taxed as income, and can force sales of family farms and businesses — but this bill addresses that with deep rate cuts on the very largest estates rather than targeted family-business relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward tax cut concentrated on a small group of large-estate heirs, with no offsetting revenue provision. Whatever force the general argument against the estate tax has, this design directs its largest benefits to estates above $10 million while the cost is spread across all federal taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Don Nickles introduced the bill on April 24, 1997, with no cosponsors [S4][S5].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote after the referral; the bill expired with the Congress on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers kept the existing estate tax rates and the revenue they raise; heirs of very large estates did not get the cut. The bill was never seriously advanced — it drew zero cosponsors and no committee action.

for.name: Sen. Don Nickles
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Estate Tax Reduction Act of 1997 and delivered introductory remarks for it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors and no votes, so no party-line pattern can be measured; the bill simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would have cut their tax rates sharply — 20% up to $10 million and 30% above, versus top rates up to 55% [S3]. Because the bill died, they continue paying the higher graduated rates.
A lower, flatter estate tax with a $1 million filing exemption [S3] would shrink demand for estate-tax planning and administration services.
